hubs.label: Sciences
hubs.intro: The natural and formal sciences, from mathematics and computing to physics, astronomy, engineering and medicine.

hubs.label: Humanities
hubs.intro: The study of human societies, cultures and beliefs.

hubs.label: Arts
hubs.intro: The visual and performing arts, music and film.

hubs.label: Explore
hubs.intro: Ways to browse the whole wiki at once: the Graph of every page, joined by links and shared tags.

hubs.label: Modern Science
hubs.intro: Modern Science holds the encyclopedia of today's sciences, humanities and arts: each topic has an Overview and one tab per subpage, and the Graph joins every page by its links and shared tags.

hubs.label: Architecture of Sacred Sciences & Wisdom
hubs.intro:
*Number, geometry, stars, sound, and the old pictures of the cosmos.*

Division A of the taxonomy groups the theoretical sacred sciences: the traditions that described the structure of the cosmos through stars, number, geometry and sound, and that linked the heavens to the human body and to buildings. Several of them are ancestors of modern astronomy, mathematics and medicine; see [[sacred-sciences.medieval-astronomy]] and [[harmonics.pythagorean-harmony]].

hubs.label: Interactions: Magic & Grimoires
hubs.intro:
*Ritual traditions, magical handbooks, folk practice, and the objects made to act in the world.*

Division B of the taxonomy groups the operative arts built on that picture of the cosmos: divination, alchemy, ceremonial magic and its handbooks, folk magic and witchcraft, and the making of talismans and ritual objects. The pages describe these practices as historians, anthropologists and folklorists study them.

hubs.label: Esoteric Schools & Traditions
hubs.intro:
*Historical lineages, mystical philosophies, and ancient initiatory cults.*

Division C of the taxonomy groups the historical, cultural and philosophical lineages that developed and preserved these ideas over millennia: the Western esoteric currents, the mystical and tantric traditions of Asia and the Islamic world, and the mystery cults and wisdom literature of the ancient civilisations.

hubs.label: Arcanum Science
hubs.intro: Arcanum Science is a historical and cultural encyclopedia of esoteric traditions, organised by the Esoteric Arcanum master taxonomy: A, the sacred sciences and their pictures of the cosmos; B, magic, divination and the grimoires; C, the schools and traditions that kept them. The pages describe what these traditions taught and how scholars study them; they are not instructions for practice.

hubs.label: Projects
hubs.intro: Projects are interactive sites of this library: the Chronos simulators of cycles across scales and the Sacred Geometry explorer.

topics.label: Math
topics.intro: Mathematics is the study of quantity, structure, space and change using precise definitions and proof. It is both a language for the sciences and a field of pure inquiry. See also [[cs.algorithms]] and [[physics.classical]].

pages.title: Algebra
pages.md:
Algebra studies operations and the structures they form, from solving equations to groups, rings and fields. Symbols stand for unknown or arbitrary quantities.

- Related: [[math.number-theory]], [[cs.cryptography]]

pages.title: Calculus
pages.md:
Calculus studies change and accumulation through derivatives and integrals, both defined with limits. It underlies much of physics and engineering.

- Related: [[physics.classical]], [[eng.mechanical]]

pages.title: Geometry
pages.md:
Geometry studies shapes, sizes and the properties of space. It ranges from Euclid's axioms to curved spaces used in relativity.

- Related: [[astronomy.cosmology]], [[art.visual]]

pages.title: Number theory
pages.md:
Number theory studies the integers, especially primes and divisibility. Once considered purely abstract, it now supports modern cryptography.

- Related: [[cs.cryptography]], [[math.algebra]]

pages.title: Probability and statistics
pages.md:
Probability models uncertainty; statistics uses data to estimate quantities and test claims. Together they support experiments, medicine and machine learning.

- Related: [[medicine.epidemiology]], [[cs.machine-learning]]

pages.title: Logic and foundations
pages.md:
Logic studies valid reasoning and the foundations on which mathematics is built, including sets and formal proof. It is closely tied to computation.

- Related: [[cs.theory]]

topics.label: Computer Science
topics.intro: Computer science studies computation, information and the systems that process them. It combines theory, engineering practice and the study of human use. See also [[math.logic]] and [[eng.electrical]].

pages.title: Algorithms and data structures
pages.md:
An algorithm is a finite procedure for solving a problem; data structures organise information so algorithms can use it efficiently. Analysis compares cost as inputs grow.

- Related: [[cs.theory]], [[math.number-theory]]

pages.title: Theory of computation
pages.md:
The theory of computation asks what can be computed at all and at what cost. It defines models such as Turing machines and classes such as P and NP.

- Related: [[math.logic]]

pages.title: Operating systems and networks
pages.md:
Operating systems manage hardware, memory and processes; networks let machines exchange data using layered protocols such as the internet protocol suite.

- Related: [[eng.electrical]], [[cs.security]]

pages.title: Machine learning
pages.md:
Machine learning builds models that improve from data rather than from explicit rules. Methods range from linear regression to large neural networks.

- Related: [[math.probability]], [[cs.nlp]]

pages.title: Natural language processing
pages.md:
Natural language processing lets software read, translate and generate human language, combining linguistics with statistical and neural methods.

- Related: [[anthropology.linguistic]], [[cs.machine-learning]]

pages.title: Cryptography
pages.md:
Cryptography protects information with mathematics: encryption keeps data private, signatures prove origin and hashes detect change.

- Related: [[math.number-theory]], [[cs.security]]

pages.title: Security
pages.md:
Computer security protects systems and data against misuse. It covers threat modelling, access control, secure design and incident response.

- Related: [[cs.cryptography]], [[cs.systems]]

topics.label: Physics
topics.intro: Physics studies matter, energy, space and time and the laws that relate them. Theories are tested by measurement and expressed mostly in mathematics. See also [[math.calculus]] and [[astronomy.cosmology]].

pages.title: Classical mechanics
pages.md:
Classical mechanics describes the motion of bodies under forces, from projectiles to planets, using Newton's laws and their later reformulations.

- Related: [[math.calculus]], [[eng.mechanical]]

pages.title: Thermodynamics
pages.md:
Thermodynamics relates heat, work and energy and introduces entropy, which sets the direction of spontaneous processes.

- Related: [[eng.chemical]], [[medicine.physiology]]

pages.title: Electromagnetism
pages.md:
Electromagnetism unifies electricity, magnetism and light in Maxwell's equations. It underlies circuits, radio and optics.

- Related: [[eng.electrical]], [[astronomy.observation]]

pages.title: Quantum mechanics
pages.md:
Quantum mechanics describes matter and light at atomic scales, where energy comes in discrete amounts and outcomes are predicted as probabilities.

- Related: [[math.probability]], [[cs.cryptography]]

pages.title: Relativity
pages.md:
Special relativity links space and time for observers in relative motion; general relativity describes gravity as the curvature of spacetime.

- Related: [[math.geometry]], [[astronomy.cosmology]]

pages.title: Particle and nuclear physics
pages.md:
Particle physics studies the elementary constituents of matter and their interactions; nuclear physics studies the atomic nucleus, its decay and energy release.

- Related: [[physics.quantum]], [[medicine.imaging]]

topics.label: Astronomy
topics.intro: Astronomy is the study of objects and phenomena beyond Earth, from planets to the large-scale structure of the universe. See also [[physics.relativity]] and [[chronos.ancient]].

pages.title: Solar system
pages.md:
The solar system consists of the Sun, eight planets, their moons and smaller bodies such as asteroids and comets, all bound by the Sun's gravity.

- Related: [[physics.classical]]

pages.title: Stars and stellar evolution
pages.md:
Stars shine by nuclear fusion. Their mass decides their lifetime and end state, from white dwarfs to neutron stars and black holes.

- Related: [[physics.particles]]

pages.title: Galaxies
pages.md:
Galaxies are vast systems of stars, gas and dark matter. The Milky Way is one of billions in the observable universe.

- Related: [[astronomy.cosmology]]

pages.title: Cosmology
pages.md:
Cosmology studies the origin, history and large-scale structure of the universe. The Big Bang model with an expanding space is the standard framework.

- Related: [[physics.relativity]], [[math.geometry]]

pages.title: Observational astronomy
pages.md:
Astronomers observe across the electromagnetic spectrum with telescopes on the ground and in space, and increasingly with gravitational waves and neutrinos.

- Related: [[physics.electromagnetism]], [[eng.aerospace]]

topics.label: Engineering
topics.intro: Engineering applies science and mathematics to design, build and maintain useful systems under constraints of cost, safety and materials. Each major field below is a subpage. See also [[physics.classical]].

pages.title: Civil engineering
pages.md:
Civil engineering designs and maintains the built environment: bridges, buildings, roads, water supply and drainage.

- Related: [[physics.classical]]

pages.title: Mechanical engineering
pages.md:
Mechanical engineering covers machines, engines, heat transfer and the mechanics of solids and fluids.

- Related: [[math.calculus]], [[physics.thermo]]

pages.title: Electrical engineering
pages.md:
Electrical engineering deals with the generation, transmission and use of electricity, and with electronics and signal processing.

- Related: [[physics.electromagnetism]], [[cs.systems]]

pages.title: Chemical engineering
pages.md:
Chemical engineering designs processes that turn raw materials into products at scale, such as fuels, medicines and plastics.

- Related: [[physics.thermo]]

pages.title: Software engineering
pages.md:
Software engineering is the disciplined design, testing and maintenance of software, including requirements, architecture and review.

- Related: [[cs.algorithms]], [[cs.security]]

pages.title: Aerospace engineering
pages.md:
Aerospace engineering designs aircraft and spacecraft, combining aerodynamics, propulsion, materials and control.

- Related: [[astronomy.observation]], [[physics.classical]]

pages.title: Materials engineering
pages.md:
Materials engineering links the structure of metals, ceramics, polymers and composites to their properties and processing.

- Related: [[physics.quantum]]

pages.title: Biomedical engineering
pages.md:
Biomedical engineering applies engineering to medicine: imaging devices, prosthetics, implants and tissue engineering.

- Related: [[medicine.imaging]], [[medicine.physiology]]

pages.title: Environmental engineering
pages.md:
Environmental engineering protects people and ecosystems through water treatment, waste management and pollution control.

- Related: [[eng.civil]], [[eng.chemical]]

topics.label: Medicine
topics.intro: Medicine is the science and practice of preventing, diagnosing and treating illness. This page is general education, not medical advice. See also [[eng.biomedical]] and [[anthropology.physical]].

pages.title: Physiology
pages.md:
Physiology explains how the organ systems of the body work and keep conditions stable, from circulation and breathing to hormones and the nervous system.

- Related: [[physics.thermo]], [[medicine.anatomy]]

pages.title: Anatomy
pages.md:
Anatomy describes the structure of the body, from organs and tissues down to cells. Imaging and dissection are its main tools.

- Related: [[medicine.imaging]]

pages.title: Genetics
pages.md:
Genetics studies how traits are inherited through DNA and how variants influence health. Sequencing has made genomes routine data.

- Related: [[anthropology.physical]], [[math.probability]]

pages.title: Epidemiology and public health
pages.md:
Epidemiology studies how disease is distributed in populations and what causes it; public health uses the findings to protect communities.

- Related: [[math.probability]]

pages.title: Medical imaging
pages.md:
Imaging lets clinicians see inside the body without surgery, using X-rays, ultrasound, magnetic resonance and nuclear methods.

- Related: [[physics.particles]], [[eng.biomedical]]

pages.title: Pharmacology
pages.md:
Pharmacology studies how drugs act on the body and how the body handles them, which underpins dosing and safety testing.

- Related: [[eng.chemical]]

topics.label: Anthropology
topics.intro: Anthropology studies human beings across time and place: their bodies, languages, cultures and material remains. Its subfields share a comparative, evidence-based approach. See also [[chronos.prehistory]] and [[beliefs.religion-studies]].

pages.title: Cultural anthropology
pages.md:
Cultural anthropology describes and compares how groups of people organise daily life, kinship, exchange and meaning. Its main method is ethnography: long-term participant observation.

- Key ideas: culture, kinship, ritual, exchange
- Related: [[beliefs.religion-studies]], [[anthropology.linguistic]]

pages.title: Biological anthropology
pages.md:
Biological anthropology examines human evolution, variation and the behaviour of other primates. It draws on genetics, anatomy and the fossil record.

- Related: [[medicine.genetics]], [[chronos.prehistory]]

pages.title: Archaeology
pages.md:
Archaeology reconstructs past societies from the objects, buildings and landscapes they left behind. Excavation, dating methods and careful recording of context are central.

- Related: [[chronos.ancient]], [[anthropology.cultural]]

pages.title: Linguistic anthropology
pages.md:
Linguistic anthropology studies language as a social practice: how speech shapes identity, how languages change and how they relate to thought and community.

- Related: [[cs.nlp]]

pages.title: Kinship and social structure
pages.md: Kinship systems define who counts as family, who may marry whom and how rights and duties pass between generations. They differ widely between societies and are a classic subject of comparison.

topics.label: Human Belief Systems
topics.intro: Human belief systems include religions, philosophies and worldviews that give people ways to understand life, ethics and the world. This subject is described neutrally and without ranking beliefs. See also [[anthropology.cultural]].

pages.title: Study of religion
pages.md:
The academic study of religion compares beliefs, practices and institutions across traditions using history, sociology and anthropology, without judging their truth.

- Related: [[anthropology.cultural]]

pages.title: Major world religions
pages.md:
Major traditions include Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Islam, Judaism and Sikhism, along with many indigenous and local religions, each with its own texts and practices.

- Related: [[chronos.ancient]]

pages.title: Philosophy
pages.md:
Philosophy examines questions about knowledge, existence, ethics and reason using argument. Branches include metaphysics, epistemology and ethics.

- Related: [[math.logic]]

pages.title: Ethics and secular worldviews
pages.md:
Ethical traditions and secular worldviews such as humanism ground moral life in reason and shared human concerns rather than religious authority.

- Related: [[beliefs.philosophy]]

pages.title: Mythology
pages.md:
Myths are traditional stories that express a community's view of origins, nature and values. Comparative mythology studies recurring themes.

- Related: [[theater.origins]]

topics.label: Art
topics.intro: Art covers works made to be seen, with traditions that differ widely across cultures and periods. Meaning comes from technique, context and interpretation. See also [[anthropology.archaeology]].

pages.title: Painting and drawing
pages.md:
Painting and drawing build images with line, colour, light and composition. Media range from pigment on cave walls to oil and digital tools.

- Related: [[math.geometry]], [[art.movements]]

pages.title: Sculpture
pages.md:
Sculpture shapes three-dimensional form by carving, modelling or casting in materials such as stone, bronze and clay.

- Related: [[eng.materials]]

pages.title: Architecture
pages.md:
Architecture is the art and technique of designing buildings and spaces, balancing function, structure and appearance.

- Related: [[eng.civil]]

pages.title: Photography
pages.md:
Photography records light on film or sensors. It became both a documentary tool and an art form.

- Related: [[movies.cinematography]], [[physics.electromagnetism]]

pages.title: Art movements
pages.md:
An art movement is a group of artists sharing aims and style for a period, such as the Renaissance, Impressionism or Cubism.

- Related: [[chronos.modern]]

topics.label: Theater
topics.intro: Theater is live performance in which actors present a story to an audience in a shared space. It is among the oldest performing arts. See also [[music.opera-and-song]] and [[chronos.ancient]].

pages.title: Origins of theater
pages.md:
Theater grew from ritual and storytelling. Classical Athens developed tragedy and comedy in festivals honouring Dionysus.

- Related: [[beliefs.religion-studies]], [[chronos.ancient]]

pages.title: Drama and playwriting
pages.md:
Dramatic writing builds plot, character and dialogue for performance. Traditions include Greek tragedy, Shakespeare and modern realism.

- Related: [[movies.screenwriting]]

pages.title: Acting and directing
pages.md:
Actors embody characters through voice, movement and emotion; directors shape the whole production. Training methods differ between schools.

- Related: [[movies.cinematography]]

pages.title: Stagecraft
pages.md:
Stagecraft includes set, lighting, sound and costume design, which together create the world of the play.

- Related: [[eng.electrical]]

pages.title: World theatre traditions
pages.md:
Many regions have distinct forms, such as Noh and Kabuki in Japan, Sanskrit drama in India and Chinese opera.

- Related: [[anthropology.cultural]]

topics.label: Music
topics.intro: Music organises sound in time. It is found in every known culture and serves ritual, entertainment and expression. See also [[physics.electromagnetism]] and [[anthropology.cultural]].

pages.title: Music theory
pages.md:
Music theory describes how pitch, rhythm, harmony and form work together, and provides notation to write music down.

- Related: [[math.number-theory]], [[music.acoustics]]

pages.title: Acoustics and instruments
pages.md:
Acoustics explains how vibrating strings, air columns and membranes produce sound. Instrument families follow the way sound is made.

- Related: [[physics.classical]]

pages.title: Western classical music
pages.md:
Western classical music spans medieval chant to contemporary works, with periods such as Baroque, Classical and Romantic.

- Related: [[chronos.modern]]

pages.title: Jazz, rock and popular music
pages.md:
Twentieth-century popular genres grew from folk, blues and jazz traditions and were spread by recording and radio.

- Related: [[music.technology]]

pages.title: Opera and song
pages.md:
Opera combines singing, orchestra and staging to tell a story; art song and folk song set poetry to melody.

- Related: [[theater.drama]]

pages.title: Recording and music technology
pages.md:
Recording, synthesis and digital audio changed how music is made and shared, from phonographs to software instruments.

- Related: [[eng.electrical]], [[cs.algorithms]]

topics.label: Movies
topics.intro: Cinema tells stories in moving images and sound. It combines photography, writing, performance and editing. See also [[art.photography]] and [[theater.acting]].

pages.title: History of cinema
pages.md:
Cinema began in the 1890s with short films, gained sound in the late 1920s and has since moved through colour, television and digital production.

- Related: [[chronos.modern]]

pages.title: Cinematography
pages.md:
Cinematography is the art of shaping a film's image through camera, lens, lighting and composition.

- Related: [[art.photography]]

pages.title: Screenwriting
pages.md:
A screenplay sets out scenes, action and dialogue. Common structures divide a film into acts with turning points.

- Related: [[theater.drama]]

pages.title: Editing and sound
pages.md:
Editing assembles shots into a sequence and controls rhythm; sound design and score complete the viewing experience.

- Related: [[music.technology]]

pages.title: Genres and national cinemas
pages.md:
Genres such as drama, comedy, science fiction and documentary group films by convention; national cinemas reflect local histories and industries.

- Related: [[anthropology.cultural]]

topics.label: Sacred Sciences & Celestial Mechanics
topics.intro:
*Planetary alignments, stellar spheres, and ancient cosmic models.*

I Sacred Sciences & Celestial Mechanics: Astrology, Medieval Astronomy, Planetary Correspondences, Historical Cosmology.

pages.title: Astrology
pages.md:
Astrology is the old tradition of relating the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets to events and characters on Earth. It grew from Babylonian omen lists, was systematised in the Hellenistic world (Ptolemy's *Tetrabiblos*) and was taught beside astronomy until the early modern period. Modern science does not support its claims; historians study it as a key part of premodern thought.

- Related: [[divination.astrological-divination]], [[sacred-sciences.planetary-correspondences]], [[sacred-sciences.medieval-astronomy]]

pages.title: Medieval Astronomy
pages.md:
Medieval astronomy, in Latin Europe and the Islamic world, worked within the geocentric model of nested celestial spheres inherited from Aristotle and Ptolemy. Scholars refined planetary tables, built astrolabes and quadrants, and kept observatories such as Maragha and Samarkand. Their work fed directly into the Copernican revolution. See also [[astronomy.observation]].

- Related: [[sacred-sciences.astrology]]

pages.title: Planetary Correspondences
pages.md:
Planetary correspondences are the premodern tables that link each of the seven classical planets to a metal, a colour, a day of the week, plants, stones and spirits: the Sun to gold, the Moon to silver, Saturn to lead. They express the idea of a cosmos joined by sympathies, and they shaped medicine, alchemy and Renaissance natural philosophy.

- Related: [[sacred-sciences.astrology]], [[talismans.talismans]], [[western-esoteric.renaissance-magic]]

pages.title: Historical Cosmology
pages.md:
Historical cosmology covers the pictures of the universe that cultures held before modern physics: the Babylonian vault of the heavens, the Greek spheres, Hindu and Buddhist cycles of world ages, and the layered worlds of Mesoamerica. Each joined a physical picture to a moral and religious order. Compare [[astronomy.cosmology]].

- Related: [[eastern-esoteric.buddhist-cosmology]], [[mystery-schools.mesoamerica]]

topics.label: Number, Geometry & Harmonic Proportions
topics.intro:
*Mathematical blueprints, resonant ratios, and acoustic harmony.*

II Number, Geometry & Harmonic Proportions: Numerology, Sacred Geometry, Sacred Sound & Music, Pythagorean Harmony.

pages.title: Numerology
pages.md:
Numerology is the tradition of giving numbers qualitative meanings. Pythagorean schools treated numbers as principles of the world, and Hebrew gematria and Greek isopsephy read words through the number values of their letters. It is a cultural and religious practice, distinct from mathematics; see [[math.number-theory]] for the science of numbers.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.kabbalah]], [[harmonics.pythagorean-harmony]]

pages.title: Sacred Geometry
pages.md:
Sacred geometry is the belief, found in many cultures, that certain shapes and ratios (the circle, the square, the golden ratio, the Platonic solids) carry a religious or cosmic meaning. It informed the plans of temples and cathedrals and Renaissance theories of proportion. The wiki's Projects > Sacred Geometry explorer shows many of these figures. See also [[math.geometry]].

- Related: [[symbolic-architecture.sacred-architecture]], [[talismans.sigaldry]]

pages.title: Sacred Sound & Music
pages.md:
Sacred sound covers the religious uses of chant, mantra, hymn, bells and drums across traditions: Vedic recitation, Gregorian chant, Tibetan overtone singing, the Islamic call to prayer. These traditions hold that sound shapes the mind or the cosmos. Musicology and ethnomusicology study them as cultural practice. See also [[music.theory]].

- Related: [[harmonics.pythagorean-harmony]], [[mystery-schools.orphic-hymns]], [[eastern-esoteric.esoteric-buddhism]]

pages.title: Pythagorean Harmony
pages.md:
Pythagorean harmony is the ancient discovery that consonant musical intervals follow simple whole-number ratios (2:1 the octave, 3:2 the fifth), and the doctrine built on it of a *musica universalis*, the music of the spheres. Through Plato, Boethius and Kepler it became a lasting image of an ordered cosmos. See also [[music.acoustics]].

- Related: [[harmonics.numerology]], [[harmonics.sacred-sound]]

topics.label: Spatial, Symbolic & Vital Architecture
topics.intro:
*Temples, glyphs, and subtle-body equilibrium.*

III Spatial, Symbolic & Vital Architecture: Sacred Architecture, Symbols & Emblems, Esoteric Medicine.

pages.title: Sacred Architecture
pages.md:
Sacred architecture is the design of temples, churches, mosques, stupas, labyrinths and monuments as religious spaces, often aligned with the sky or laid out on symbolic proportions. Examples range from Stonehenge and the Egyptian temples to Gothic cathedrals and Angkor Wat. See also [[art.architecture]].

- Related: [[harmonics.sacred-geometry]]

pages.title: Symbols & Emblems
pages.md:
Esoteric symbols and emblems are the visual language of these traditions: alchemical signs, planetary glyphs, the pentagram, the ouroboros, the Rosicrucian rose cross, and the emblem books of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries. Art history and iconography read them as compressed images of a doctrine.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.mystical-symbolism]], [[talismans.talismans]]

pages.title: Esoteric Medicine
pages.md:
Esoteric medicine names premodern healing systems built on ideas of balance and vital force: Galenic humours, Paracelsian medicine, Ayurveda's doshas, Chinese qi and meridians. Some remedies survive in modern pharmacology; the theories behind them are studied by historians of medicine. See also [[medicine.pharmacology]].

- Related: [[alchemy.spagyrics]], [[talismans.wortcunning]], [[eastern-esoteric.taoist-alchemy]]

topics.label: Divination Systems & Epistemic Arts
topics.intro:
*Ways of reading cards, hands, signs, dreams, and the future.*

I Divination Systems & Epistemic Arts: Tarot, I Ching, Runes, Oracles, Palmistry & Chiromancy, Scrying & Crystallomancy, Geomancy, Geomantic Figures, Dream Interpretation, Oneiromancy, Classical Omens, Astrological Divination, Sortilege & Cartomancy.

pages.title: Tarot
pages.md:
The tarot is a deck of 78 cards, 22 major arcana and 56 minor, first made for card games in fifteenth-century Italy. From the late eighteenth century French and later English occultists read it as a book of symbols tied to Kabbalah and astrology, and it became the best-known divination deck. The Rider-Waite-Smith deck of 1909 set its modern imagery.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.kabbalah]], [[divination.sortilege]], [[western-esoteric.mystical-symbolism]]

pages.title: I Ching
pages.md:
The *I Ching* (Book of Changes) is a Chinese classic built on 64 hexagrams of six broken or unbroken lines, chosen by counting yarrow stalks or tossing coins. Its core dates to the Western Zhou, and Confucian commentaries made it a work of philosophy as well as divination. It shaped Chinese cosmology and was read widely in the West from the twentieth century.

- Related: [[mystery-schools.ancient-china]], [[eastern-esoteric.taoism]]

pages.title: Runes
pages.md:
Runes are the letters of the Germanic alphabets (futharks) used from about the second century CE on stone, wood and metal. Some inscriptions are charms, and Tacitus describes lot-casting with marked slips. Rune divination as practised today is largely a twentieth-century revival. Runology studies the inscriptions as language and history.

- Related: [[folk-magic.european-folk-magic]], [[talismans.sigaldry]]

pages.title: Oracles
pages.md: An oracle was a sanctuary or person through whom a god was thought to answer questions: the Pythia at Delphi, the oak of Dodona, the oracle of Amun at Siwa. Cities and rulers consulted them on war, colonies and law, so oracles were political institutions as well as religious ones. Modern 'oracle decks' borrow the name.

pages.title: Palmistry & Chiromancy
pages.md: Palmistry, or chiromancy, reads character and fortune from the lines, mounts and shape of the hand. It appears in India, China and ancient Greece, and printed manuals spread it in Renaissance Europe. Like physiognomy, it has no scientific support and is studied as a cultural practice.

pages.title: Scrying & Crystallomancy
pages.md:
Scrying is the practice of looking into a reflective or clear surface (a crystal, a black mirror, a bowl of water) to see visions. It is recorded from antiquity, and John Dee's obsidian mirror and crystal sessions in the 1580s are its most famous European case. Historians and psychologists study it as a form of visionary experience.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.enochian]], [[talismans.ritual-implements]]

pages.title: Geomancy
pages.md:
Geomancy (Arabic *'ilm al-raml*, 'the science of the sand') is a divination method that turns random marks in sand or on paper into figures of four lines each, then combines them into a chart. It spread from the Islamic world to medieval Europe and West Africa, where it is related to Ifa and Sikidy. Not to be confused with Chinese feng shui.

- Related: [[divination.geomantic-figures]]

pages.title: Geomantic Figures
pages.md:
The sixteen geomantic figures are the building blocks of a geomancy chart: each is four rows of one or two dots, giving 2x2x2x2 = 16 forms, with Latin names such as *Via*, *Populus*, *Fortuna Major* and *Carcer*. Medieval writers tied each to a planet and a sign. The same binary pattern appears in the Ifa system of West Africa.

- Related: [[divination.geomancy]]

pages.title: Dream Interpretation
pages.md:
Dream interpretation reads dreams as messages, from the Egyptian and Babylonian dream books and Artemidorus' *Oneirocritica* (second century CE) to Freud's *Interpretation of Dreams* (1899) and Jung. Modern sleep science studies dreaming in the brain; the older traditions are studied as cultural history. See also [[medicine.physiology]].

- Related: [[divination.oneiromancy]]

pages.title: Oneiromancy
pages.md:
Oneiromancy is divination by dreams, often by deliberate dream incubation: sleeping in a temple to receive a healing or prophetic dream, as at the Asclepieia of Greece. Lucid dreaming, the awareness of dreaming within a dream, is described in Tibetan dream yoga and has been measured in sleep laboratories since the 1980s.

- Related: [[divination.dream-interpretation]]

pages.title: Classical Omens
pages.md:
Classical omens are the signs read by ancient states: Babylonian omen series such as *Enuma Anu Enlil*, Etruscan and Roman haruspicy (reading the livers of sacrificed animals), and Roman augury (reading the flight of birds). Augurs were public officials, so omen reading was part of government. See also [[anthropology.archaeology]].

- Related: [[mystery-schools.ancient-rome]], [[mystery-schools.mesopotamian-wisdom]]

pages.title: Astrological Divination
pages.md:
Astrological divination covers the branches of astrology that answer questions or pick times: horary (a chart for the moment a question is asked), electional (choosing a favourable moment) and mundane or judicial astrology (forecasting for states and events). Medieval Arabic and Latin authors such as Masha'allah and Guido Bonatti wrote its main manuals.

- Related: [[sacred-sciences.astrology]]

pages.title: Sortilege & Cartomancy
pages.md:
Sortilege is divination by casting lots, dice, bones or marked objects, one of the oldest and most widespread forms; cartomancy is its later form with playing cards, popular from the eighteenth century. Both treat a chance outcome as meaningful. See also [[math.probability]] for the mathematics of chance.

- Related: [[divination.tarot]]

topics.label: Alchemical & Transformative Sciences
topics.intro:
*The mastery and transmutation of matter and soul.*

The study of transmutation and change, rooted in the Hermetic principle "as above, so below".

II Alchemical & Transformative Sciences: Spiritual Alchemy (The Magnum Opus), Spagyrics & Physical Transmutation, Sympathetic Magic.

pages.title: Spiritual Alchemy (The Magnum Opus)
pages.md:
Spiritual alchemy reads the alchemical Great Work (*Magnum Opus*), with its stages of blackening, whitening and reddening, as an allegory of inner change rather than a recipe for gold. The reading goes back to Christian and Hermetic authors and was made famous in the twentieth century by Carl Jung's studies of alchemical imagery.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.alchemy]], [[western-esoteric.hermeticism]], [[western-esoteric.rosicrucianism]]

pages.title: Spagyrics & Physical Transmutation
pages.md:
Spagyrics is the Paracelsian art of separating and recombining substances, mostly plants and minerals, to make medicines; physical transmutation is the older alchemical goal of turning base metals into gold. Laboratory techniques of the alchemists, such as distillation and sublimation, passed into early modern chemistry. See also [[eng.chemical]].

- Related: [[symbolic-architecture.esoteric-medicine]], [[western-esoteric.alchemy]]

pages.title: Sympathetic Magic
pages.md:
Sympathetic magic is the term James Frazer (*The Golden Bough*, 1890) gave to practices based on two principles: similarity (like affects like) and contagion (things once in contact stay connected). The concept shaped early anthropology and is still used to describe beliefs across cultures. See also [[anthropology.cultural]].

- Related: [[folk-magic.folk-magic]]

topics.label: Ceremonial Magic, Grimoires & Summoning Disciplines
topics.intro:
*Ritual handbooks, angelic languages, and spirit hierarchies.*

The ritual traditions and magical handbooks through which practitioners sought to address spirits and hierarchies of non-physical beings.

III Ceremonial Magic, Grimoires & Summoning Disciplines: Ceremonial Magic, Grimoires, Solomonic Magic & Literature, Enochian Magic, Theurgy (High Magic), Goetia & Binding (Low Magic), Necromancy & Dark Arts.

pages.title: Ceremonial Magic
pages.md:
Ceremonial magic is the learned, ritual magic of Western Europe: long, formal rites with divine names, circles, timing by the planets and written instructions. It runs from medieval and Renaissance manuscripts to nineteenth-century orders such as the Hermetic Order of the Golden Dawn. Historians study it as part of intellectual and religious history.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.theurgy]], [[western-esoteric.thelema]]

pages.title: Grimoires
pages.md:
A grimoire is a handbook of magic. Surviving examples range from late antique Greek magical papyri to medieval Latin manuscripts and cheap printed editions of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. They are important sources for the history of religion, medicine, print culture and popular belief.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.solomonic]]

pages.title: Solomonic Magic & Literature
pages.md:
Solomonic literature is a family of texts attributed to King Solomon, who was credited in Jewish, Christian and Islamic lore with power over spirits: the *Testament of Solomon*, the *Key of Solomon* (*Clavicula Salomonis*) and the *Lesser Key* or *Lemegeton*. The attribution is legendary; the texts date from late antiquity to the seventeenth century.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.grimoires]], [[ceremonial-magic.goetia]]

pages.title: Enochian Magic
pages.md:
Enochian is the angelic language and system recorded by the Elizabethan scholar John Dee and the scryer Edward Kelley in the 1580s, from sessions with a crystal. Dee's diaries hold its alphabet, tables and calls. The material was taken up by the Golden Dawn in the 1890s, and linguists have studied the language's structure.

- Related: [[divination.scrying]], [[western-esoteric.renaissance-magic]]

pages.title: Theurgy (High Magic)
pages.md:
Theurgy ('divine work') is the ritual side of late Neoplatonism, defended by Iamblichus around 300 CE: rites meant to unite the soul with the gods rather than to command them. It shaped Proclus, Byzantine thought and Renaissance magic, and the term was later used for 'high' as opposed to 'low' magic.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.ceremonial-magic]], [[western-esoteric.neoplatonism]], [[western-esoteric.neoplatonic-commentaries]]

pages.title: Goetia & Binding (Low Magic)
pages.md:
Goetia, from a Greek word for sorcery, names the conjuring of lesser or demonic spirits, set against theurgy. Its best-known text is the first book of the *Lemegeton* (seventeenth century), a catalogue of seventy-two spirits with their seals. Medieval clergy wrote and condemned such texts, so they are key sources for the history of demonology.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.solomonic]]

pages.title: Necromancy & Dark Arts
pages.md:
Necromancy originally meant consulting the dead, as in the *Odyssey*'s descent to Hades or the biblical Witch of Endor; in the Middle Ages the word came to mean demonic magic in general. Curse tablets (*defixiones*) of the Greco-Roman world are a related, well-documented practice. Laws and church courts treated these arts as crimes.

- Related: [[mystery-schools.greek-mysteries]]

topics.label: Folk Magic & Witchcraft Traditions
topics.intro:
*Vernacular, earth-centered, and traditional magical practices.*

Vernacular and traditional magical practices that existed outside the formal, learned traditions.

IV Folk Magic & Witchcraft Traditions: Folk Magic, European Folk Magic, Witchcraft.

pages.title: Folk Magic
pages.md:
Folk magic is the everyday magic of ordinary people: charms, blessings, cures, protective rhymes and household customs passed on by word of mouth. It existed beside official religion everywhere and is studied by folklorists and anthropologists. See also [[anthropology.cultural]].

- Related: [[alchemy.sympathetic-magic]], [[folk-magic.european-folk-magic]], [[folk-magic.witchcraft]]

pages.title: European Folk Magic
pages.md:
European folk magic includes the cunning folk of Britain, the *benandanti* of Friuli, the *Segensprüche* of German-speaking lands, Scandinavian *svartkonst* books, and seasonal rites such as midsummer fires. Trial records and charm books preserve much of it. Historians such as Carlo Ginzburg and Owen Davies have studied it in depth.

- Related: [[divination.runes]], [[folk-magic.folk-magic]]

pages.title: Witchcraft
pages.md:
Witchcraft has two histories. One is the early modern European witch hunts (about 1450-1750), in which tens of thousands were tried and many executed under a learned theory of devil worship. The other is modern Wicca and related movements, founded in England in the 1950s, which present witchcraft as a nature religion. See also [[beliefs.religion-studies]].

- Related: [[folk-magic.folk-magic]], [[talismans.wortcunning]]

topics.label: Talismanic & Applied Arcanum
topics.intro:
*Objects, sigils, and botanicals made to act in the world.*

Esoteric theory applied to physical objects: the realm of the craftsman.

V Talismanic & Applied Arcanum: Talismans, Amulets & Sigils, Protective Amulets, Ritual Implements, Sigaldry & Warding, Artifice & Enchantment, Wortcunning (Esoteric Herbology).

pages.title: Talismans, Amulets & Sigils
pages.md:
Talismans are objects made at a chosen time and inscribed with signs to draw a benefit; amulets are worn to protect; sigils are signs standing for a spirit or a wish. The *Picatrix*, an Arabic manual translated into Latin in the thirteenth century, is the classic text on astrological talismans. Museums hold many examples from every period.

- Related: [[sacred-sciences.planetary-correspondences]], [[symbolic-architecture.symbols-emblems]], [[talismans.protective-amulets]]

pages.title: Protective Amulets
pages.md:
Protective amulets are worn or hung to ward off misfortune: the Egyptian eye of Horus, the Mediterranean and Middle Eastern *nazar* against the evil eye, the *hamsa* hand, horseshoes and red threads. They are among the most common archaeological finds and remain part of daily life in many places. See also [[anthropology.archaeology]].

- Related: [[talismans.talismans]]

pages.title: Ritual Implements
pages.md:
Ritual implements are the tools of religious and magical rites: wands, knives, cups, censers, bells, mirrors and the inscribed disc or pentacle. In the Western ceremonial tradition the wand, cup, sword and pentacle were linked to the four elements and to the four suits of the tarot. Their forms are studied as material culture.

- Related: [[divination.scrying]], [[talismans.artifice]]

pages.title: Sigaldry & Warding
pages.md:
Sigaldry, from an Old Norse word for charm, names the inscribing of protective or powerful signs, and warding the marking of places against harm. Examples include apotropaic marks carved near doors and hearths in old English buildings, Icelandic staves such as the *Aegishjalmur*, and protective hex signs on Pennsylvania barns.

- Related: [[harmonics.sacred-geometry]], [[divination.runes]]

pages.title: Artifice & Enchantment
pages.md:
Artifice and enchantment describe the old idea that made things (swords, rings, automata, statues) can hold a power of their own. It runs through legend and literature: the Hermetic animated statues of the *Asclepius*, the swords of the Arthurian and Norse sagas, the golem of Prague. Historians of technology note how such stories tracked real automata.

- Related: [[talismans.ritual-implements]]

pages.title: Wortcunning (Esoteric Herbology)
pages.md:
Wortcunning, an old English word for knowledge of plants, covers the lore of herbs used for healing, protection and ritual: mandrake, vervain, rue, mugwort. Medieval herbals mixed practical botany with planetary and magical correspondences. Some of these plants are pharmacologically active and many are toxic. See also [[medicine.pharmacology]].

- Related: [[symbolic-architecture.esoteric-medicine]], [[folk-magic.witchcraft]]

topics.label: Western Esoteric Traditions
topics.intro:
*Hermetic, Gnostic, Kabbalistic, and related currents of the Western tradition.*

I Western Esoteric Traditions: Hermeticism, Alchemy, Kabbalah, Gnosticism, Neoplatonism, Rosicrucianism, Esoteric Christianity, Christian Mysticism, Thelema, Theosophy, Western Esotericism, Neoplatonic Commentaries, Renaissance Magic, Mystical Symbolism.

pages.title: Hermeticism
pages.md:
Hermeticism is the tradition based on texts attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a Greek-Egyptian sage, written in Roman Egypt in the first centuries CE: the *Corpus Hermeticum* and the *Asclepius*. Their Latin translation by Marsilio Ficino in 1471 made them central to Renaissance thought, until Isaac Casaubon dated them in 1614.

- Related: [[alchemy.spiritual-alchemy]], [[western-esoteric.renaissance-magic]], [[mystery-schools.egyptian-mysteries]]

pages.title: Alchemy
pages.md:
Alchemy is the tradition of transforming matter, practised in Greco-Roman Egypt, the Islamic world (Jabir ibn Hayyan), China and Latin Europe. Its aims included making gold, medicines and the elixir of life. Historians now see it as a direct ancestor of chemistry: Robert Boyle and Isaac Newton both worked on it. See also [[eng.chemical]].

- Related: [[alchemy.spiritual-alchemy]], [[alchemy.spagyrics]]

pages.title: Kabbalah
pages.md:
Kabbalah is the Jewish mystical tradition that took shape in twelfth- and thirteenth-century Provence and Spain, with the *Zohar* as its central text, and was reshaped by Isaac Luria in sixteenth-century Safed. Its diagram of ten *sefirot*, the Tree of Life, describes the divine emanations. Christian Kabbalah adapted it from the Renaissance on.

- Related: [[harmonics.numerology]], [[divination.tarot]], [[western-esoteric.rosicrucianism]]

pages.title: Gnosticism
pages.md:
Gnosticism is the modern name for religious movements of the second and third centuries that taught salvation through *gnosis*, a revealed knowledge, often with a myth of a lesser creator god. The Nag Hammadi library, found in Egypt in 1945, gave scholars their own texts for the first time. See also [[beliefs.world-religions]].

- Related: [[western-esoteric.esoteric-christianity]]

pages.title: Neoplatonism
pages.md:
Neoplatonism is the last great school of Greek philosophy, founded by Plotinus (third century CE): all things emanate from the One, through Intellect and Soul, and the soul can return to it by contemplation. Through Porphyry, Proclus and later Christian, Jewish and Islamic thinkers it shaped medieval and Renaissance metaphysics. See also [[beliefs.philosophy]].

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.theurgy]]

pages.title: Rosicrucianism
pages.md:
Rosicrucianism began with three anonymous German manifestos (1614-1616) announcing a secret brotherhood of the Rosy Cross devoted to reform through Christian Hermetic and alchemical knowledge. No such order is known to have existed then, but the texts started a long debate and inspired later societies from the eighteenth century onward.

- Related: [[alchemy.spiritual-alchemy]], [[western-esoteric.kabbalah]]

pages.title: Esoteric Christianity
pages.md:
Esoteric Christianity is a name for readings of Christianity that claim a hidden, inner teaching beside the public one. Examples include Christian Kabbalah, the theosophy of Jacob Boehme, Swedenborg's visions and Rudolf Steiner's Anthroposophy. Church history generally treats these as movements on the edge of mainstream doctrine.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.gnosticism]], [[western-esoteric.christian-mysticism]]

pages.title: Christian Mysticism
pages.md:
Christian mysticism is the tradition of contemplative prayer seeking direct experience of God, within the churches themselves: Pseudo-Dionysius, Meister Eckhart, the *Cloud of Unknowing*, Teresa of Avila, John of the Cross and the Hesychasts of Eastern Orthodoxy. Its writings are classics of religious literature.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.esoteric-christianity]]

pages.title: Thelema
pages.md:
Thelema is the religious philosophy founded by the English writer Aleister Crowley after he dictated *The Book of the Law* in Cairo in 1904. Its central idea is that each person should find and follow their True Will. It is studied by historians of new religious movements and modern occultism.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.ceremonial-magic]], [[western-esoteric.western-esotericism]]

pages.title: Theosophy
pages.md:
Theosophy is the movement of the Theosophical Society, founded in New York in 1875 by Helena Blavatsky, Henry Olcott and William Judge. It taught a hidden wisdom behind all religions and helped bring Hindu and Buddhist ideas to Western audiences; its headquarters moved to Adyar, India. It strongly influenced modern esotericism and art.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.western-esotericism]], [[eastern-esoteric.tantra-vedanta]]

pages.title: Western Esotericism
pages.md:
Western esotericism is the academic field that studies, as history, the currents on this page and its neighbours: Hermeticism, Kabbalah, alchemy, Rosicrucianism, occultism and New Age. Antoine Faivre and Wouter Hanegraaff helped found it as a university discipline from the 1990s. See also [[beliefs.religion-studies]].

- Related: [[western-esoteric.thelema]], [[western-esoteric.theosophy]]

pages.title: Neoplatonic Commentaries
pages.md:
The Neoplatonic commentaries are the long expositions of Plato and Aristotle written by late antique philosophers such as Proclus, Simplicius and Olympiodorus, and later by Renaissance scholars such as Ficino. They preserved much of ancient philosophy and joined it to theology, both pagan and Christian.

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.theurgy]]

pages.title: Renaissance Magic
pages.md:
Renaissance magic is the learned 'natural magic' of fifteenth- and sixteenth-century Europe: Marsilio Ficino's astral medicine, Pico della Mirandola's union of Kabbalah and philosophy, Cornelius Agrippa's *Three Books of Occult Philosophy* (1533) and Giordano Bruno. Frances Yates' studies made it a major theme of intellectual history.

- Related: [[sacred-sciences.planetary-correspondences]], [[ceremonial-magic.enochian]], [[western-esoteric.hermeticism]]

pages.title: Mystical Symbolism
pages.md:
Mystical symbolism is the use of images to express religious or esoteric ideas that are hard to say in words: alchemical allegories, emblem books, the tarot's trumps, the Tree of Life, mandalas. It influenced Symbolist painting and poetry of the late nineteenth century. See also [[art.movements]].

- Related: [[symbolic-architecture.symbols-emblems]], [[divination.tarot]]

topics.label: Eastern Esoteric Traditions
topics.intro:
*Mystical and tantric currents of Asia and the Islamic world.*

II Eastern Esoteric Traditions: Sufism, Tantra & Vedanta, Taoism, Esoteric Buddhism, Kashmir Shaivism, Sufi Mysticism, Taoist Alchemy, Tantric Manuscripts, Buddhist Cosmology.

pages.title: Sufism
pages.md:
Sufism is the mystical tradition of Islam, organised from about the twelfth century into orders (*tariqas*) such as the Qadiriyya, Naqshbandiyya and the Mevlevi, whose turning ceremony is famous. Sufis practise remembrance of God (*dhikr*), follow a master and wrote much of the great poetry of Arabic, Persian and Turkish. See also [[beliefs.world-religions]].

- Related: [[eastern-esoteric.sufi-mysticism]]

pages.title: Tantra & Vedanta
pages.md:
Vedanta is the family of Hindu philosophies based on the Upanishads; Advaita Vedanta, set out by Shankara (eighth century), teaches that the self and the ultimate reality, *brahman*, are one. Tantra names ritual traditions, Hindu, Buddhist and Jain, that arose from about the fifth century CE, using mantra, diagram and initiation.

- Related: [[western-esoteric.theosophy]], [[eastern-esoteric.kashmir-shaivism]], [[eastern-esoteric.tantric-manuscripts]], [[mystery-schools.ancient-india]]

pages.title: Taoism
pages.md:
Taoism (Daoism) is the Chinese tradition rooted in the *Tao Te Ching* attributed to Laozi and in the *Zhuangzi*, teaching harmony with the Tao, the way of nature. From the second century CE it also became an organised religion with priests, temples, scriptures and rites. See also [[beliefs.world-religions]].

- Related: [[divination.i-ching]], [[eastern-esoteric.taoist-alchemy]]

pages.title: Esoteric Buddhism
pages.md:
Esoteric Buddhism, or Vajrayana, is the tantric form of Buddhism that arose in India around the seventh century and spread to Tibet, Mongolia, China and Japan, where it became the Shingon and Tendai schools. It uses mantra, mandala, visualisation and initiation by a teacher. It is the main form of Buddhism in Tibet.

- Related: [[harmonics.sacred-sound]], [[eastern-esoteric.buddhist-cosmology]], [[eastern-esoteric.tantric-manuscripts]]

pages.title: Kashmir Shaivism
pages.md:
Kashmir Shaivism is a group of non-dual Hindu traditions that flourished in Kashmir from the ninth to the twelfth century, with Abhinavagupta as its greatest thinker. It teaches that the world is the free self-expression of Shiva as pure consciousness, with *spanda*, the divine vibration, as a key idea. It also produced an important theory of aesthetics.

- Related: [[eastern-esoteric.tantra-vedanta]]

pages.title: Sufi Mysticism
pages.md:
Sufi mysticism is the inner teaching of Sufism: the path through stations (*maqamat*) and states (*ahwal*) towards *fana*, the passing away of the ego in God. It is expressed in the writings of al-Ghazali and Ibn Arabi and the poetry of Rumi, Attar and Hafez, which are classics of world literature.

- Related: [[eastern-esoteric.sufism]]

pages.title: Taoist Alchemy
pages.md:
Taoist alchemy has two branches: external alchemy (*waidan*), the making of elixirs from minerals, which poisoned several Chinese emperors, and internal alchemy (*neidan*), which from the Tang and Song dynasties turned the same language into meditation and breathing practice. Joseph Needham's work traced its links to Chinese science.

- Related: [[symbolic-architecture.esoteric-medicine]], [[eastern-esoteric.taoism]]

pages.title: Tantric Manuscripts
pages.md:
Tantric manuscripts are the large body of texts, in Sanskrit and other languages, that record tantric doctrine and ritual: the subtle body with its channels and chakras, mantras, and diagrams (*yantras* and *mandalas*). Many survive in Nepalese and Tibetan collections and are being catalogued by scholars.

- Related: [[eastern-esoteric.tantra-vedanta]], [[eastern-esoteric.esoteric-buddhism]]

pages.title: Buddhist Cosmology
pages.md:
Buddhist cosmology describes a universe of countless world systems, each with Mount Meru at its centre and realms ranging from hells to the heavens of the gods, arranged by states of mind. Beings move through them in the cycle of rebirth. It is set out in texts such as the *Abhidharmakosha*. Compare [[astronomy.cosmology]].

- Related: [[eastern-esoteric.esoteric-buddhism]], [[sacred-sciences.historical-cosmology]]

topics.label: Mystery Schools & Ancient Wisdom
topics.intro:
*The civilizations and initiatory cults behind the oldest religious and philosophical literature.*

III Mystery Schools & Ancient Wisdom: Egyptian Mysteries, Greek Mysteries, Mesopotamian Wisdom, Mithraism, Ancient Persia, Ancient Rome, Ancient India, Ancient China, Mesoamerica, Eleusinian Mysteries, Mesopotamian Religion, Orphic Hymns, Ancient Initiation.

pages.title: Egyptian Mysteries
pages.md:
Egyptian religion had temple priesthoods, secret rites and an elaborate literature of the afterlife: the Pyramid Texts, the Coffin Texts and the *Book of the Dead*. Greek and Roman writers saw Egypt as the home of hidden wisdom, an image later Hermeticism and Freemasonry drew on. Egyptology studies the actual sources. See also [[anthropology.archaeology]].

- Related: [[western-esoteric.hermeticism]], [[mystery-schools.ancient-initiation]]

pages.title: Greek Mysteries
pages.md:
The Greek mysteries were cults that admitted members by secret initiation and promised a better fate after death: those of Eleusis, Samothrace, Dionysus and the Orphics. Initiates were forbidden to reveal the rites, so modern knowledge comes from hints in literature, inscriptions and art. See also [[beliefs.mythology]].

- Related: [[ceremonial-magic.necromancy]], [[mystery-schools.eleusinian]], [[mystery-schools.orphic-hymns]]

pages.title: Mesopotamian Wisdom
pages.md:
Mesopotamian scholars of Sumer, Babylon and Assyria kept vast cuneiform libraries of omens, astronomy, medicine and incantation, such as that of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh. Their systematic records of the sky laid foundations for later astronomy and astrology. See also [[astronomy.observation]].

- Related: [[divination.classical-omens]], [[mystery-schools.mesopotamian-religion]]

pages.title: Mithraism
pages.md:
Mithraism was a Roman mystery cult of the god Mithras, popular among soldiers from the first to the fourth century CE. Members met in cave-like temples (*mithraea*) whose central image shows Mithras slaying a bull, and they rose through seven grades of initiation linked to the planets. Little of its doctrine was written down.

- Related: [[mystery-schools.ancient-persia]], [[mystery-schools.ancient-rome]]

pages.title: Ancient Persia
pages.md:
Ancient Persia is the home of Zoroastrianism, the religion of Zarathustra, with its sacred texts the *Avesta*, its opposition of truth and the lie, and its priests, the Magi. It was the state religion of the Achaemenid and Sasanian empires and shaped ideas of judgement and the end of time. See also [[beliefs.world-religions]].

- Related: [[mystery-schools.mithraism]]

pages.title: Ancient Rome
pages.md:
Roman religion was a state matter: priestly colleges read omens by augury, the Sibylline Books were consulted in crises, and the empire absorbed cults from Egypt, Persia and Asia Minor, such as those of Isis, Mithras and Cybele. This mixing is called syncretism and is a major theme of the history of religions.

- Related: [[divination.classical-omens]], [[mystery-schools.mithraism]]

pages.title: Ancient India
pages.md:
Ancient India produced the Vedas (from about 1500 BCE), hymns for sacrificial ritual, and the Upanishads, philosophical texts on the self and *brahman*. Ascetic and yogic movements of the first millennium BCE gave rise to Buddhism and Jainism. See also [[beliefs.philosophy]].

- Related: [[eastern-esoteric.tantra-vedanta]]

pages.title: Ancient China
pages.md:
Ancient China's earliest writing appears on Shang dynasty oracle bones (about 1200 BCE), used to put questions to ancestors. Shamans (*wu*), the *I Ching*, and the cosmological schools of yin and yang and the five phases shaped Chinese thought before and alongside Confucianism and Taoism. See also [[anthropology.archaeology]].

- Related: [[divination.i-ching]]

pages.title: Mesoamerica
pages.md:
Mesoamerican civilisations, Olmec, Maya and Aztec among them, built complex calendar systems (the 260-day ritual count and the 365-day year), tracked Venus and eclipses, and aligned cities to the sky. Their cosmology placed the present world in a series of created and destroyed ages. See also [[astronomy.observation]].

- Related: [[sacred-sciences.historical-cosmology]]

pages.title: Eleusinian Mysteries
pages.md:
The Eleusinian Mysteries were held each year at Eleusis near Athens for nearly two thousand years, in honour of Demeter and her daughter Persephone. Initiates fasted, walked in procession from Athens and saw secret rites in the hall of the Telesterion, which promised a happier afterlife. Emperor Theodosius closed the sanctuary at the end of the fourth century.

- Related: [[mystery-schools.greek-mysteries]], [[mystery-schools.ancient-initiation]]

pages.title: Mesopotamian Religion
pages.md:
Mesopotamian religion honoured gods such as Anu, Enlil, Enki, Inanna/Ishtar and Marduk in city temples and ziggurats. Its myths include the *Epic of Gilgamesh* and the creation poem *Enuma Elish*, among the oldest literature in the world. See also [[beliefs.mythology]].

- Related: [[mystery-schools.mesopotamian-wisdom]]

pages.title: Orphic Hymns
pages.md:
The Orphic Hymns are 87 short Greek hymns, probably from the second or third century CE, attributed to the mythical poet Orpheus. Orphic texts more broadly taught that the soul is divine and bound in a cycle of rebirth; gold tablets buried with initiates give instructions for the afterlife. See also [[music.western-classical]] for Orpheus in later music.

- Related: [[harmonics.sacred-sound]], [[mystery-schools.greek-mysteries]]

pages.title: Ancient Initiation
pages.md:
Initiation rites mark the passage from one state to another, often by symbolic death and rebirth. Arnold van Gennep's *Rites of Passage* (1909) described their three stages of separation, transition and incorporation, and anthropologists have found them in many societies, as well as in the ancient mystery cults. See also [[anthropology.cultural]].

- Related: [[mystery-schools.egyptian-mysteries]], [[mystery-schools.eleusinian]]

topics.label: Chronos
topics.intro: Chronos is the timeline of human history, from the first tools to the present. Periods are conventions that help organise a continuous story. See also [[anthropology.archaeology]].

pages.title: Prehistory
pages.md:
Prehistory covers the time before writing, from stone tools about 3 million years ago through the spread of Homo sapiens and the start of farming.

- Related: [[anthropology.physical]], [[anthropology.archaeology]]

pages.title: Ancient world
pages.md:
The ancient world saw the first cities and states, in Mesopotamia, Egypt, the Indus valley, China and later Greece and Rome, with the invention of writing.

- Related: [[theater.origins]], [[beliefs.world-religions]]

pages.title: Middle ages
pages.md:
The middle ages, roughly 500 to 1500 CE in Europe, saw feudal states, the growth of universities and wide trade networks linking Europe, Africa and Asia.

- Related: [[beliefs.world-religions]]

pages.title: Early modern period
pages.md:
From about 1500 to 1800, exploration, printing, the scientific revolution and the Enlightenment reshaped knowledge, trade and politics.

- Related: [[physics.classical]], [[beliefs.philosophy]]

pages.title: Modern era
pages.md:
The modern era brought industrialisation, mass education, world wars, decolonisation and the digital revolution.

- Related: [[eng.electrical]], [[cs.systems]], [[movies.history]]
